description: We’re a group of Engineering Students and Technology enthusiasts building innovative solutions with modern web technologies. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we’re exploring the Earth Information Jukebox through frontend, backend, data visualization, Web Audio API, data processing, UI/UX, machine learning, APIs, and creative technology to turn Earth Science data into meaningful interactive sound.
summary: Prism Tone is an “Earth Jukebox” that lets people hear our changing planet. It takes real NASA climate data (temperature, wind, precipitation, ice, wildfire, vegetation) and turns it into calm, musical sound, month by month, on an interactive world map. Live captions explain every note in plain words, so the data can be understood by listening, reading, or both. It is built for blind and low-vision users, deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and anyone who finds charts hard to read. User can also upload a NASA image and hear it as sound.
details:
The problem

NASA’s Earth Information Center makes beautiful visuals, but they are built for the eyes. A person who cannot see a map or a color chart is locked out of the story. And even for sighted people, a graph of numbers rarely makes you feel how the planet is changing.

What we built

Prism Tone is a web app where you pick a place on a world map, pick a year or a range of years, and press play. The climate data for that place becomes music.

- Interactive map. Click any continent or search any country (by typing or speaking). The map shows the real value for the month you select.

- Data becomes sound. Temperature controls pitch, rainfall controls how busy the rhythm is, and wind controls the weight and brightness of a low drone. Up to three datasets can play together as layers.

- Music, not noise. Every note is snapped to a musical scale, so it sounds pleasant. When a month is warmer than normal, the music shifts to a more tense, minor feel. When it is cooler, it opens up.

- Live captions and transcript. Each month gets a plain-language caption: the value, how it compares with normal, and what the sound is doing. Captions stay visible even with the volume at zero. The full session can be copied or downloaded as a text file.

- Waveform and graphs. You can watch the sound as a live waveform, see the full 45-year series, and inspect any point. A data table is available for screen readers.

- Listen to an image. You can give the app a NASA image. Our backend reads it as a grid of pixels (color, brightness, edges) and turns it into a musical score, so a picture can be heard too.

- Accessibility settings. Large caption sizes, high contrast, reduced motion, optional vibration, a “Describe this view” button for screen readers, and full keyboard control (Space, arrows, C, T and more).

How it works

1. Data comes from the NASA POWER API (and is cached so the demo stays reliable).

2. Our Python/FastAPI backend cleans the data, scales it, and turns it into a simple “musical score” (which notes, how long, how loud).

3. The same pipeline handles images: pixels become sound events, which are then simplified into the same kind of score.

4. In the browser, Tone.js plays the score with soft pads, a gentle lead, reverb and a limiter so it stays calm and never harsh.

5. If our backend is offline, the app falls back to a built-in mapping so it still works.

We never invent data. If a month is missing, it stays silent and the caption says so. Estimated values and brightness-based image readings are clearly labelled.

Who it helps

Blind and low-vision users, deaf and hard-of-hearing users (captions and waveform), students and teachers, and anyone who wants to feel climate change instead of just reading about it.

What we’d build next

- A Braille view: send captions to a separate page, save them, and export a printable PDF/BRF file.

- Fire, water-storage and vegetation layers (NASA FIRMS, GRACE, MODIS) once complete data is available.

- Pulling colour-chart legends from NASA images so image sounds map to real values, not just brightness.

- More spatial audio and user-defined sound mappings.

Tech

React, Vite, Tailwind, Tone.js / Web Audio, OpenCV, MapLibre, Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Pandas, NASA POWER.
